This is the video for module one of Fintech Fundamentals.
Fintech, short for financial technology, means using software, phones and data for paying, saving, borrowing, insuring and sending money.

say: For decades, a bank account needed a branch visit, a utility bill and a reference letter. Branches were in cities, so every visit cost transport and lost trading time.

panel.heading: Why banks left so many people out

say: Minimum balances ate into small savings, and products were designed for salaried workers, not market women with daily cash flows.

panel.heading: Why banks left so many people out

say: Unfamiliar forms put people off, and some had lost money before. Each barrier looks small. Together they made formal finance too costly.

panel.heading: Why banks left so many people out

say: Safaricom launched M-Pesa in Kenya in 2007. The key idea was not the phone. It was the agent, a shop owner who swaps cash for electronic value and back again.

Cash-in at one agent, send by phone number, cash-out at another. In Nigeria, growth came through USSD codes, bank apps, POS agents at almost every junction, and wallets like Opay, PalmPay and Moniepoint.
For example, Halima sells grains in a village market about 25 km from the nearest bank branch.

card.title: What an agent changes for Halima

say: A return bus trip costs her about 3,000 naira, and she loses half a day of sales, about 5,000 naira of profit.

say: Then a POS agent opens near the market. Depositing three times a week at about 100 naira each costs about 1,200 naira a month. That saving, not the app, is the real inclusion benefit.

say: Every app sits on shared plumbing called payment rails. The sender types the 10-digit account number, called the NUBAN, and the app returns the account name.

say: Next, she enters her PIN, and her provider checks her balance and fraud rules. NIBSS, the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System, routes the instruction through its instant service, NIP.

say: The receiving bank credits the account in seconds. Banks do not move cash for each transfer. They settle the net amounts at the Central Bank of Nigeria later. That is why a failed but debited transfer usually reverses after checks.

say: For example, Amaka in Onitsha sends 20,000 naira to her supplier Tunde. Under the CBN charge bands in use for several years, her bank may charge up to 25 naira.

cards.d: 20,000 naira falls in the 5,001 to 50,000 band, so her bank may charge up to 25 naira.
Tunde received 10,000 naira or more, so a 50 naira levy may be deducted, leaving 19,950.
25 plus 50 is 75 naira, about 0.375% of the payment. Rules change, so check the current guide.

say: A fintech is a business. It earns from fees per payment, and from fees split with agents on cash-out.
It earns an interest spread on loans. And wallet money, called float, must be held at licensed banks, separate from the company's own money, where it can earn interest if rules allow.

Free transfers are the door, and bills, cards and loans are the rooms behind it. A company that pays 1,000 naira to win a user who earns it 50 naira a month needs 20 months just to recover that bonus.

To remember. Judge inclusion on access, usage and quality, not account counts. The agent network made mobile money work. Always confirm the account name before you send. And growth without healthy unit economics does not last.
